title: Getting to know exam practice
description: A short paper to try everything out: an information page, a short essay, a calculation and a multiple-choice question.
instructions:
This paper is a tour of the way online exams work. Nothing is marked by a person: try every button.

  • The time starts when you press Start. The time left is shown at the top left, under your candidate number.
  • Your answers are saved as you type. There is no Save button.
  • As in Inspera’s exam browser, you can copy and paste within the exam (from your answers or from the questions), but text copied from anywhere else – another tab, a website, your notes – cannot be pasted in.
  • Move between the questions with the arrows at the bottom right, or with the numbered tiles along the bottom.
  • When you have finished, go to the submission page (the ✔ tile) and press Submit now.

questions.title: How this paper works
questions.text:
An online exam shows one question at a time. Look around the screen:

  • At the top: your candidate number, the time remaining, whether your answers are saved, the resources you may use (here a calculator and two slides) and the options menu ☰. The menu changes the text size and the contrast, hides the time, switches the spelling checker on or off, and takes you to the submission page.
  • Along the bottom: a tile for each question. A bar along the top of a tile means the question has an answer; a little flag means you have flagged it to come back to. The i tile is this page. The ✔ tile on the right is the submission page: it turns purple when every question has an answer.
  • In an essay: the toolbar has bold, italic and underline, sub- and superscripts, lists, tables, special characters (Ω), formulas (Σ), drawings and backup copies of your answer. Alt+F10 takes you to the toolbar from the keyboard. The word count is under the box.

Press the arrow at the bottom right to go to the first question.

questions.title: A tissue under the microscope
questions.text:
Open one of the two slides in the resources at the top of the page (the lung or the small intestine). It opens in the Microscope tab: look at it at low and at high power, then come back to Exam practice.

Describe what you see, and explain how the structure of the tissue suits its function.

You may add a labelled sketch with the drawing tool (the pencil in the toolbar).

At most 300 words: you cannot type more than that.
questions.guidance:
A good answer names the tissue, describes it from low to high power, and links each feature to the function.

Lung: a very large number of thin-walled air spaces (alveoli) give a huge surface area; the wall between air and blood is very thin (type I pneumocytes, a thin basement membrane and capillary endothelium), so diffusion distances are short; a dense network of capillaries keeps the concentration gradients steep; type II pneumocytes make surfactant; bronchioles and blood vessels can be seen between the alveoli; elastic fibres help the lungs to recoil.

Small intestine: the mucosa is folded into finger-like villi (and the cells have microvilli), which give a large surface area for absorption; a single layer of columnar epithelium (enterocytes) gives a short distance to the blood capillaries and lacteals in the core of each villus; goblet cells make mucus; crypts between the villi hold the dividing cells that replace the epithelium; smooth muscle in the muscularis externa mixes and moves the contents (peristalsis).

Marks for: correct identification (1); accurate description of the main layers or features (4); links between structure and function (4); clear writing within the word limit (1). A labelled drawing can earn the description marks.

questions.title: Real size from a scale bar
questions.text:
On a printed micrograph of a blood smear, the scale bar represents 50 µm and is 20 mm long. A red blood cell on the same micrograph measures 3.0 mm across.

What is the real diameter of the red blood cell, in micrometres (µm)?
questions.guidance:
The magnification is the size on the picture divided by the real size: 20 mm = 20 000 µm, so the magnification is 20 000 µm ÷ 50 µm = ×400.

Real size = size on the picture ÷ magnification = 3.0 mm ÷ 400 = 3000 µm ÷ 400 = 7.5 µm.

Change everything into the same units before you divide.

questions.title: Magnification
questions.text: Which of these gives the real size of something seen in a micrograph?
options: Real size = size in the micrograph × magnification
Real size = size in the micrograph ÷ magnification
Real size = magnification ÷ size in the micrograph
Real size = size in the micrograph − magnification
questions.guidance: Magnification = size in the image ÷ real size, so real size = size in the image ÷ magnification. A magnification of ×400 makes things 400 times larger, so you divide by 400 to get back to the real size.
